data: Second US Mars surface lander (Utopia Planitia 1976-09-03). Twin of Viking 1 lander; ran biology, soil chemistry + meteorology until 1980

The surface half of NASA's Viking 2 mission and the second successful US Mars lander, 47 days after Viking 1. Launched 1975-09-09 on a Titan IIIE-Centaur, touched down at Utopia Planitia (47.97° N, 134.04° E) on 1976-09-03 — much further north than Viking 1, in a different plains type to broaden the science return. Ran the same instrument suite as Viking 1: a biology package (Pyrolytic Release / Labeled Release / Gas Exchange experiments looking for microbial metabolism — the famously ambiguous Labeled Release positive that remains debated), GC-MS for soil organics (none detected), facsimile cameras returning > 1,400 images, X-ray fluorescence soil chemistry, meteorology, and seismometer (one of two ever flown on Mars — unable to detect quakes through cabin noise). Operated until 1980-04-11 when batteries failed.
First successful Mars lander; biology experiments
Lost during landing in 1999; the failure led NASA to review its “faster, better, cheaper” approach
Confirmed water ice in Martian soil
Last successful Soviet Moon mission — returned 170 g of Mare Crisium regolith 1976-08-22; last lunar sample return until Chang'e 5

Operated 1,281 days at 48°N — the highest-latitude Mars surface mission until Phoenix. Detected the first frost on Mars in September 1977 — water ice confirmed — with an iconic high-resolution image captured in May 1979. The lander's biological experiments returned the same ambiguous results as Viking 1's: chemistry that mimicked metabolism, but without unambiguous biology.
Viking Lander Flight Capsule 3, a flight-built Viking lander that never flew
